metadata.note: deep-explainer, fresh technical build covering CI/CD and deployment practices on GCP: GitHub Actions, Pull Requests, dev/staging/production environments, Docker, Kubernetes (importance + GKE setup), and the three deployment strategies (Rolling/Blue-Green/Canary) with use cases, pros, and cons. 4 acts: I GitHub Actions + PRs (the gate), II environments (the promotion path), III Docker + Kubernetes (package + orchestrate; GKE setup), IV deployment strategies (how you actually ship). Content is general, well-established DevOps/cloud engineering practice -- deliberately hedged away from version numbers, pricing, or GCP console screenshots per DOUBLE-CHECK LAW (see FACTCHECK.md). No Manim on this machine (pangocairo not installed) -- MANIM lane absorbed into REMOTION. VOX quota: 5 real Wikimedia Commons photographs, metaphor imagery. BinaryBranch/DivergentFates hero beats planned up front at A1-4, A2-3, A2-5, A4-3, A4-4 for clean 9:16 Short derivation. Signed for Divyank from authoring time. GATE P: PENDING, see PEDAGOGY.md.

beats.narration_text: Salaam — this is Liam, in for Divyank. A pull request that passes every review can still break production the moment it deploys — because merging code and shipping code are two completely different problems, solved by two completely different systems. Let's build the whole pipeline, GCP-shaped, end to end.

show.event: composer cold-opens, spark + 'Salaam, Liam' greeting settles
command types itself in: the merging-vs-shipping question
send arms, runningText plays
RESULT lines land in sequence

props.command: Build me the full CI/CD and deployment pipeline on GCP: GitHub Actions, pull requests, environments, Docker, Kubernetes, and how you actually roll out a new version.
output: merging and shipping are two different gates
the same image gets promoted, never rebuilt
rolling, blue-green, and canary trade off differently

beats.act: Act I — From Commit to Pipeline
beats.narration_text: Every change to a real production system passes through a checkpoint first — not a suggestion, an actual gate a human and a machine both have to clear before it goes any further.

shot.prompt: real archival border-checkpoint photo -- illustrative of a pull-request gate, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A1-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push toward the checkpoint booth
serif label lands: 'an actual gate, not a suggestion'

beats.act: Act I — From Commit to Pipeline
beats.narration_text: Branch protection is what makes this real instead of optional. Require the status check, and a red workflow blocks the merge outright. Skip that one setting, and 'the tests passed' is just a comment somebody has to remember to read.

show.event: question card: 'is the status check required?'
two outcomes: required / optional

data.question: Is the status check actually required?

branches.label: Required
branches.detail: a red workflow blocks the merge

branches.label: Not required
branches.fix: someone has to remember to read it

resolver.label: One setting decides which
resolver.detail: branch protection, not the workflow file itself

beats.act: Act II — Three Environments, One Path
beats.narration_text: The same build gets handed off three times before it ever reaches a real user — and the whole discipline is refusing to rebuild it at each handoff.

shot.prompt: real archival relay-race photo -- illustrative of promoting a build through environments, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A2-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push along the handoff
serif label lands: 'never rebuilt at the handoff'

beats.act: Act II — Three Environments, One Path
beats.narration_text: Rebuild the container at every environment, or promote the exact same image forward. Rebuilding risks a different artifact reaching production than the one staging actually tested. Promoting the same image is the only way the test that passed is the thing that ships.

show.event: question card: 'rebuild, or promote the same image?'
two outcomes: rebuild / promote

data.slideMeta: build once, or rebuild per environment
data.question: Rebuild per environment, or promote the same image?

branches.label: Rebuild each time
branches.detail: a different artifact can reach production
branches.fix: staging never really tested what shipped

branches.label: Promote the same image
branches.detail: the tested bytes are the shipped bytes

resolver.label: Build once, deploy many
resolver.detail: the rule underneath every environment strategy

beats.act: Act II — Three Environments, One Path
beats.narration_text: Same code, deployed to staging first, versus skipped straight to production. Staging surfaces the config error, the missing environment variable, the integration that only breaks under production-like load — before a real customer ever sees it.

show.event: two tracks diverge: staging-first arcs down good, skip-to-prod arcs up warn

tracks.label: Skipped straight to production
tracks.outcome: the config error, live, on real traffic

tracks.label: Through staging first
tracks.outcome: the same error, caught before a customer sees it

beats.narration_text: A container solves one specific problem: the same image runs identically on a laptop, in staging, and in production — no more 'it works on my machine.'

shot.prompt: real archival shipping-container photo -- illustrative of Docker containers, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A3-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow drift along the container stacks
serif label lands: 'no more works-on-my-machine'

beats.narration_text: Autopilot, or Standard? Autopilot: Google manages the nodes, you manage workloads only, less control. Standard: you manage the node pools directly yourself, full control, more operational work. Both run the exact same Kubernetes API underneath.

show.event: question card: 'Autopilot, or Standard?'
two outcomes: Autopilot / Standard

resolver.label: Same Kubernetes API, either way
resolver.detail: the choice is about who runs the nodes

beats.act: Act IV — How You Actually Ship It
beats.narration_text: Even with a tested image and a running cluster, one decision is still yours: how new code actually replaces old code, while real users are on the line.

shot.prompt: real archival traffic-light photo -- illustrative of gradually shifting traffic during a rollout, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A4-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push onto the signal
serif label lands: 'while real users are on the line'

beats.act: Act IV — How You Actually Ship It
beats.narration_text: Rolling's honest tradeoff: no extra infrastructure, no downtime, built into Kubernetes natively. But old and new versions serve real traffic side by side during the rollout, and there's no single-switch instant rollback.

show.event: question card: 'rolling — what do you get, what do you give up?'
two outcomes: pro / con

data.question: Rolling — what do you get, what do you give up?

branches.label: You get
branches.detail: no extra infrastructure, no downtime, native to K8s

branches.label: You give up
branches.detail: old and new serve traffic together mid-rollout

beats.act: Act IV — How You Actually Ship It
beats.narration_text: Blue-Green's honest tradeoff: one switch, and rollback is exactly as instant — flip straight back to blue. But you're running double the infrastructure during the cutover, and a database migration doesn't get to enjoy that same instant rollback.

show.event: two tracks diverge: the switch-forward arcs up good, the cost arcs down warn

data.splitLabel: what you get / what it costs

tracks.label: What you get
tracks.outcome: instant rollback — flip straight back to blue

tracks.label: What it costs
tracks.outcome: double infrastructure; DB migrations don't roll back instantly
